# Measuring and Checking

A model is not finished when it looks finished. It is finished when the
dimensions you care about are correct and the parts do not collide. This
chapter is the inspection pass.

## What you will learn

- How to measure bodies and selections.
- How to check clearance and interference.
- How to verify square, spacing, and alignment.
- How to use sections to see inside an assembly.

## Measure the body first

Start with the coarse facts:

- bounding box;
- volume;
- surface area;
- centre of mass;
- face, edge, and vertex counts.

The bounding box catches wrong planes and wrong overall lengths. Volume catches
missing or doubled features. Face counts are a quick warning that a boolean
left a sliver or split a face into many fragments.

For a 90 × 90 × 2400 mm post, the bounding box should be exactly that, and the
volume should be about 19.44 × 10⁶ mm³. If the volume is 9.72 × 10⁶ mm³, the
profile was half the intended area.

## Measure selections

You can measure more than whole bodies:

- the length of an edge;
- the area of a face;
- the position of a vertex;
- the diameter of a circle or cylinder;
- the distance between two faces, edges, or points;
- the centre-to-centre distance between two holes.

This is how you check a bolt pattern, a picket gap, or the diagonal of a gate.
Measure the geometry you will actually use on site, not a dimension that only
exists in the sketch.

## Clearance and interference

Two different questions:

- **Interference:** do two bodies overlap? Even a tiny overlap is a problem if
  the parts are supposed to be separate.
- **Clearance:** how close are two bodies that do not overlap? A gate that
  misses its post by 0.5 mm is technically clear and practically useless.

Run both checks on moving parts and on assemblies that will be built from
separate pieces. Contact between two boards that are meant to touch is fine;
contact between a door and its frame is not.

## Checking square

For a rectangular frame, measure both diagonals. Equal diagonals mean the frame
is square, assuming the opposite sides are equal. This is the same 3-4-5
logic you use on site, applied to the model.

For a fence run, check:

- post spacing at the top and bottom;
- the overall run length;
- the offset of each post from the datum line;
- the diagonal of each bay if the ground is sloped.

## Sections

A section cuts the model and shows the inside. Use it to check:

- whether a tenon bottoms out in a mortise;
- whether a bolt passes through both members;
- whether a notch is deep enough;
- whether a roof plane meets a wall plate cleanly.

A section is also a useful figure for the book: it explains a joint better than
an exterior view.

## Common failures

| Symptom | Likely cause | Check |
|---------|--------------|-------|
| Bounding box is rotated | Sketch on the wrong plane | Plane and normal |
| Volume is half | Open or duplicated profile | Profile status |
| Parts overlap slightly | Nominal sizes used instead of actual | Material dimensions |
| Gate binds | No clearance in the model | Clearance check |
| Hole misses | Wrong face or datum | Hole position from a known edge |
| Diagonal differs | Frame out of square | Both diagonals |
| Body count too high | Cuts leaving slivers | Face/body list |

## Build along: inspect the gate

1. Open the half-lap gate from Chapter 7.
2. Measure the overall width, height, and thickness.
3. Measure both diagonals.
4. Run an interference check on the frame and brace.
5. Run a clearance check between the gate and its posts through the swing arc.
6. Cut a section through one lap and confirm the joint depth.
7. Save the checks as a short list in the chapter.

## Checks

- Overall dimensions match the design brief.
- Diagonals are equal within your tolerance.
- No unintended interference.
- Moving parts have clearance through their full travel.
- Sections show the intended joint depth.
- Units are still millimetres.

## Exercises

1. Measure the diagonal of a 2400 × 1800 mm fence panel. What should it be?
2. Check the clearance between a 1000 mm gate and a 90 mm post at 90° open.
3. Find an accidental overlap in a model you have already built.
4. Measure the distance from a bolt hole centre to the nearest edge. Compare it
   with the fastener manufacturer's minimum.

## Next

Once the model is correct, it has to communicate. The next chapter turns it
into figures, sections, and a takeoff you can take to the shop.
